processing: A long decoction of many dried herbs, roots and flowers. The count varies from around 10 to 28 or more, and each shop adjusts its own recipe.
harvest_season: Not applicable: a blended decoction, made all year.
appearance_dry: A coarse mix of dried roots, bark, stems, leaves and flowers.
appearance_liquor: As with most shop liangcha, close to black and nearly opaque.
appearance_wet: Dark, softened herbs, normally strained off before serving.
taste_profile: Strongly bitter and medicinal, the standard for hard Cantonese herbal tea, with a slight sweet return in some blends.

brewing.notes: Generally bought ready-made. For a herb pack, follow the pack; a low simmer of about half an hour is the usual liangcha method.

vintage_note: No vintages: it is a same-day drink at liangcha counters or a dated pack of mixed herbs. Since shops rarely post the ingredients, ask what is in it, especially if you are on medication.
description:
Nian Si Wei, better known in English as 24 Flavors and in Cantonese as ya sei mei, is one of the most representative Cantonese herbal teas, and among the most bitter. Despite the name there is no tea leaf, and quite possibly not 24 ingredients either.

It is a folk recipe rather than a classical formula, so the count floats: some shops use a little over ten, others go to 28. Ingredients often cited include mulberry leaf, chrysanthemum, honeysuckle, bamboo leaf, Microcos leaf and Ilex rotunda.

Drink it for what it is: a hard, dark, bitter cup taken warm in small amounts. It is not a tea to sip for pleasure on a first try, and milder liangcha like Five Flower Tea are an easier way in.

The mix is strongly cooling by the logic of Chinese medicine and rarely disclosed at the counter. It is considered unsuitable in pregnancy and for those with a cold constitution, and people on Western medicine or prone to drug allergies are advised to avoid it. Many Chinese medicine doctors do not recommend taking it without a diagnosis.
history:
24 Flavors came from folk practice in Guangdong rather than from old medical texts, which is why it has no set formula. Its spread is tied to working people, for whom a doctor's visit was a luxury and a bowl from the herbal tea shop stood in for one.

Today it remains a fixture of Cantonese liangcha counters, though its old role as an everyday remedy is viewed more critically.
